results.summary: This design implements a six-digit seven-segment clock displaying hours, minutes and seconds. Two active-high pushbuttons increment hours and minutes for setting the time, and the decimal points blink once per second. It requires a 32768 Hz clock, a six-digit common-anode display, and six PMOS/PNP digit-enable transistors. The outputs include active-low segment drives and multiplexed digit enables, and the design is intended for breadboard or custom PCB assembly.

This design provides an SPI interface that converts serial input into 8-bit parallel output on the uo pins. The documentation states that an SPI interface is used, but does not describe the SPI mode, bit order, or register map. Testing requires an external SPI master such as an RP2040 board, and no other external hardware is specified. The documentation is thin and leaves key implementation details undefined.

This project is an SPI device that provides a GPIO and memory interface. It uses dedicated pins for SPI MOSI, clock and chip select, with MISO, debug, system clock mirror and status outputs. Testing is done with an external USB-to-SPI adapter such as an MCP2210 board, and no other external hardware is required. The documentation refers to a readme file that is not included here, so the register map and protocol details remain unspecified.

This design adds two 4-bit numbers and displays the sum on a seven-segment display. Inputs are set using DIP switches on the upper and lower nibbles, and an always block maps the sum to display segments. If the sum cannot be shown on the display, a dot is shown instead, and overflow is not handled. The design is a straightforward arithmetic demonstration with no external hardware beyond the switches and display.

This project provides a single high-speed comparator built with SiGe NPN heterojunction bipolar transistors. It compares two analog inputs and outputs a mostly-digital signal, with power gating controlled by a digital enable pin. Testing involves setting the enable high, applying analog signals between 0.0 V and 1.2 V to the inputs, and observing the output. No external hardware is required, but the documentation notes that the comparator should be disabled when not in use because there is no power gating.

This design contains a rough 24-bit VGA DAC with a digital control block for testing different modes. It outputs analog RGB signals on ua pins and digital sync and blanking signals, and includes various test patterns selectable via input mode pins. Silicon test reports indicate that some patterns are fine, some are distorted, and the VGA screen occasionally loses sync, but the analog output looked good in scope shots. It requires a VGA monitor and likely a Tiny VGA PMOD for connection.

This design is a VGA clock demo that shows a bouncing ball animation over an adaptation of Matt Venn's VGA clock. It produces 640x480 60Hz VGA timing with RGB222 colour outputs compatible with the Tiny VGA PMOD. Inputs allow adjusting hours, minutes, and seconds, and selecting between Tiny VGA and Matt's VGA Clock PMODs. It requires a 25 MHz clock, a VGA monitor, and the appropriate PMOD, and the seconds timer assumes an exact 25.000 MHz clock.

This design includes a simple digital counter that can be driven by either an external clock or an internal ring oscillator. Data is loaded through a shift interface, and the counter runs as fast as possible to produce a result that can be read back. Testing involves selecting the internal clock, loading a starting value and cycle count, and observing that the output is the starting value plus the counter value. An oscilloscope is recommended to measure the actual speed, and the ring oscillator frequency divided by 16 is expected to be between 12.5 MHz and 25 MHz.

This design displays a bouncing ROOTS logo with a kaleidoscope background and an animated colour gradient on a VGA monitor. It is configured through input pins, though the documentation does not specify what each input controls. The design requires a VGA monitor and a Tiny VGA PMOD for connection. It is a visual demo with no other external hardware requirements.

This design is a visual demo that shows a hypnotic prism floating in a starry night on a VGA monitor. It has no control inputs and simply runs when connected to a VGA display. The design requires a VGA monitor and a Tiny VGA PMOD interface. The documentation is minimal and provides no additional details about the implementation or testing.
